name: LMDeploy (TurboMind)
notable_features: Two engines behind one toolkit: TurboMind (C++/CUDA) and a pure-Python PyTorchEngine that the README offers explicitly to lower the barrier to rapid experimentation. That pairing is unusual and useful
Developed by the MMRazor/MMDeploy team, so it inherits an OpenMMLab lineage and a compression-first identity that most serving frameworks do not have
Persistent batch (their term for continuous batching), blocked KV cache, automatic prefix caching
Compressed weights: AWQ W4A16 with a claimed 2.4x over FP16, plus online int8/int4 KV-cache quantization added April 2024
MXFP4 support on NVIDIA GPUs from V100 upward, and llm-compressor 4-bit symmetric/asymmetric support added February 2026
A request-distribution service for multi-model, multi-machine, multi-card serving - a proxy layer rather than a single-process server
Model zoo is InternLM-centric but covers Llama, Qwen (including MoE variants), InternVL2, GLM, Gemma, DeepSeek and multimodal VLMs
TurboMind got the EuroSys 2027 paper (arXiv:2508.15601), which is unusual for a serving framework and indicates real systems research
8106 stars, v0.18.0 released 2026-09-28, last push 2026-09-28, 2271 open issues
hardware_caveats: ALL PERFORMANCE FIGURES IN THE README ARE VENDOR CLAIMS with no methodology. Read them as positioning: 'up to 1.8x higher request throughput than vLLM'; 4-bit '2.4x higher than FP16'; MXFP4 '1.5x the performance of vLLM on H800 for openai gpt-oss models'; the April 2024 GQA upgrade taking InternLM2-20B to 16+ RPS, 'about 1.8x faster than vLLM'. Every one names a different model, so none of them compose into a general statement about the engine
The vLLM comparisons are the ones to distrust least and still not trust: vLLM tunes itself against the same popular models, so a per-model win usually means a configuration win

Effectively CUDA-first. The README's own backends list is CUDA/ROCm/CPU/Mac in the sense of an aspiration; the substantive work - MXFP4 from V100, AWQ, KV-cache quantization, CUDA graphs - is NVIDIA-specific. No NPU, no Metal-accelerated generation path, no Vulkan
Version line is still v0.x at v0.18.0 despite being five years old, which is the honest maturity signal
2271 open issues is the largest backlog in this slice. Part of that is the InternLM model zoo's own churn
Windows support is documented only at tp=1 (from the 2023/08 news item) - single-GPU only
Model coverage skews InternLM and Qwen. Outside that zoo the compatibility burden is real
Two engines means two behaviour sets: a bug or a perf difference may be TurboMind-specific or PyTorchEngine-specific
best_for: Deployment if you are in the InternLM/Qwen ecosystem, where this is the best-tuned option and the model support is first-class
Compression-forward serving: AWQ, MXFP4 and KV-cache quantization are supported together here in a way most engines do not coordinate
Running a proxy in front of many models across many machines, via the request-distribution service
Reading a TurboMind paper (EuroSys 2027) on mixed-precision inference - one of very few serving frameworks with a peer-reviewed systems paper
Fast experimentation with the pure-Python PyTorchEngine when you do not want a C++ build
avoid_for: Deciding on vendor speed claims - there is no methodology and the model changes with every claim
Non-NVIDIA hardware. This is a CUDA-first engine in practice
Production without reading the support matrix; v0.18.0 with 2271 open issues is a moving target
notes: The strongest niche candidate in this slice that is neither dead nor a research prototype, and a genuinely distinct third way between vLLM and llama.cpp: a compression-first C++ engine from the OpenMMLab lineage with a EuroSys paper. TurboMind paper arXiv:2508.15601 (2025-08-21) verified via the arXiv API. All metadata from the GitHub API on 2026-10-03.
